messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

At thirty-five, Minh had been a UX designer for a decade, a profession that demanded he anticipate how people would move through digital spaces, what they would click, where they would hesitate. His own life had come to feel like a poorly designed interface, one where every delay signaled a system failure. The trouble had begun three years earlier, when a routine physical revealed a mass on his kidney. The biopsy, the surgery, the weeks of waiting for pathology results—these had unfolded with a clinical efficiency that only made them more terrifying. He remembered the way the surgeon’s voice had dropped, just slightly, when he said the word “malignant.” Minh had survived; the cancer was caught early, and treatment was considered successful. But something in him had not survived intact.

He had come to believe there was something fundamentally wrong with him, a defect that the cancer had merely exposed. This conviction settled into his bones during the months of follow-up scans, when he would sit in the waiting room and watch other patients flip through magazines, and he would feel a hollow numbness, as though the person sitting there was not really him. He was certain he was weak—weaker than his wife, who had held his hand through every appointment, weaker than the other survivors he saw in online forums who posted about gratitude and new leases on life. Minh felt dead inside, and he was sure this proved his weakness, which in turn proved his defectiveness. These appraisals became the lens through which he saw everything.

Because he was defective and weak, Minh began to avoid anything that might remind him of his vulnerability. He stopped driving past the hospital where he had been treated, taking a longer route to work that added twenty minutes to his commute. When his wife suggested they watch a medical drama, he left the room without explanation. Physical examinations became impossible: at his annual checkup, he told the doctor he was fine and walked out before the nurse could take his blood pressure. Even thinking about the event felt dangerous, as though the memory itself could trigger a recurrence. He would redirect his mind when the thoughts surfaced, focusing on the pixel-level details of a wireframe or the precise shade of a button color. This avoidance felt necessary, a way to keep the fear contained.

But the fear was not contained. Minh’s body remained on constant alert, his shoulders perpetually tight, his jaw clenched even in sleep. He found it impossible to trust safety: when his oncologist told him his scans were clean, Minh heard the words but felt nothing—no relief, no release—only the certainty that the doctor was wrong, or that the cancer was simply hiding. This threat monitoring bled into every corner of his life. When a colleague was late to a meeting, Minh’s mind immediately supplied the worst-case scenario: a stroke, a seizure, an ambulance. Delays of any kind—a subway stalled between stations, a package that did not arrive on time, a restaurant that took too long to bring the check—triggered a visceral sense that something bad was happening. He could not sit still; he would tap his foot, check his phone, pace the room. The world felt like a trap that could spring at any moment.

The threat, in turn, reinforced his negative appraisals. Each time his body went on alert, he interpreted it as further proof that he was broken. A normal person, he told himself, would have moved on. A normal person would not feel this way. His weakness was confirmed daily, and his defectiveness became a self-evident truth. The loop tightened: he felt defective, so he avoided; he avoided, so the threat grew; the threat grew, so he felt more defective. At work, he began to avoid any project that involved health-related content, claiming a conflict of interest. His manager noticed his reluctance to collaborate on a new app for a hospital system and reassigned him to a less visible project. Minh felt the relief of the avoidance, but also the sting of confirmation: he was not capable, not reliable, not whole.

What finally brought him to seek help was a moment so mundane it felt absurd. He was waiting for his coffee at a café, and the barista was taking too long. His heart began to pound, his vision narrowed, and he had to leave before the drink was made, walking out into the cold air with his hands shaking. He stood on the sidewalk and realized he could not keep living this way—always waiting for the disaster that never came, always certain it was coming anyway. He made an appointment with a therapist, afraid that even talking about it would break him, but more afraid of what he had already become.
